opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underappreciated aspects of adversarial machine learning, and honestly of security in general. The order of moves matters enormously.

In the standard setup, the defender goes first. You build your model, you publish your defense, you deploy your system, and then the attacker gets to look at exactly what you did and adapt to it. That's a huge asymmetry. The defender has to anticipate every possible attack in advance, and the attacker only has to find one thing that works against the specific defense in front of them. This is why so many published adversarial example defenses have been broken, often within weeks. The defense was evaluated against the attacks that existed when it was written, not against an attacker who knows how the defense works and designs something specifically to get around it.

So when I evaluate a defense, the main question I ask isn't "does this stop existing attacks?" It's "what happens when someone who knows exactly how this works tries to break it?" That's the adaptive attack setting, and it's the only one that really matters, because it's the one you'll face in the real world.

There are some cases where the order flips, and they're interesting. Take data poisoning, or the image-cloaking tools people built to protect their photos or artwork from being trained on. There the "attacker", the person perturbing their images, has to commit first. They publish the perturbed image, and it sits on the internet forever. The model trainer can come along a year later with a better model, a new training method, or a robust feature extractor that ignores the perturbation. The person who perturbed the image can't go back and update it. So in that setting the defender, the trainer, gets the second-mover advantage, and that's a really bad position for those protection tools. You're making a static bet against all future progress in machine learning.

The general lesson I'd draw is that whoever moves second, and whoever can keep adapting, usually wins. If you're designing a system, figure out which side of that you're on. If you're forced to commit to something static while the other side adapts, you need to be very skeptical about how long your protection will last, and you should be honest with users about that rather than offering a false sense of security.

For LLMs this plays out right now with jailbreaks and prompt injection. Model developers ship a model, and then thousands of people get unlimited tries to find a prompt that works. The developer can patch, so it's more of a repeated game than a one-shot one, but each round the attacker still gets to see the latest defense and respond. That's why I'm wary of claims that some filter or fine-tuning trick has "solved" jailbreaks. Show me it surviving a motivated adaptive attacker over time, and then I'll believe it.

r001.rationale: It says the attacker only needs to find one attack that works against the specific defense in front of them, rather than anticipate every possible defense.

r002.rationale: It explains that after a defense is deployed, attackers can inspect how it works and design an attack to get around it.

r003.rationale: It describes data poisoning and image-cloaking as cases where the attacker commits first, while the trainer can later choose improved methods that counter the published data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually something I think about a lot, because I think it's one of the most important structural facts about the whole field, and it's one that people who come to AI security from the machine learning side often don't appreciate at first.

The basic point is that in almost every security setting, the defender has to move first. The defender builds the system, ships it, publishes the paper, puts the model behind an API, whatever it is. And then the attacker gets to look at that thing and decide what to do. The attacker gets to sit there for as long as they want, try a thousand things, and they only have to find one that works. The defender has to anticipate everything in advance and get all of it right. So the asymmetry isn't just that attacking is easier than defending in some abstract sense, it's that the order of play hands the attacker an enormous informational advantage. They are responding to a fixed target, and the defender is guessing about an adversary that doesn't exist yet.

And you can see this play out really concretely in adversarial examples. For years, people would propose a defense, they'd evaluate it against the attacks that existed at the time, and it would look great. Then someone like me would come along afterward, read the paper, understand exactly how the defense works, and design an attack specifically for it. And it would fall over. Not because the authors were dumb or careless, but because they were in the impossible position of defending against an attack that hadn't been written yet, while I got to write an attack against a defense that was fully specified in front of me.

Now, the thing that I think is interesting is that the order isn't totally fixed. There are ways defenders try to flip it. The classic one is secrecy, right, don't tell the attacker how the defense works. And in traditional security we've mostly learned that this is a bad idea, because the secret leaks eventually and then you have no defense at all. But there's a more legitimate version, which is randomness or adaptivity, where the defender gets to make some choices after the attacker has committed. If the defense has a random component that's resampled every time, in some sense the defender is moving second for that particular interaction. That's actually part of why things like randomized smoothing or certain cryptographic approaches are appealing, they try to reclaim some of that second-mover advantage.

The other way the order matters is at the ecosystem level rather than the individual system level. If I find an attack and publish it, now I've moved first and the defenders get to respond to my fixed, published attack. So the research community sort of alternates who's moving first. And I think that's actually healthy. The reason I spend so much of my time breaking things is that I'd much rather the first person to adaptively attack a defense be me, writing a paper about it, than someone who actually wants to cause harm. If I move first on the attack side, the defender gets to see it and learn from it before it matters.

Where I get a bit more worried is with language models specifically, because the deployment loop is so fast and the attack surface is so wide. A model gets deployed, millions of people are poking at it, and anything anyone finds gets shared immediately. So the defender has moved first on an enormous scale, and there's a huge number of attackers all moving second simultaneously. The dynamics there are, I think, even less favorable to the defender than they were in the adversarial examples world, and I don't think we've really figured out what to do about that yet.

r001.rationale: The response says the attacker can study the fixed, fully specified defense and design an attack specifically for it, while the defender must anticipate attacks in advance.

r002.rationale: It explains that an attacker can read a defense paper after publication, understand how the defense works, and then design an attack against it.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss data poisoning or describe the attacker publishing poisoned training data before the defender chooses a defense.

astra-6.text:
I think the order matters a lot. There’s a big difference between asking whether a defender can stop an attack they’ve already seen and asking whether an attacker can break a defense that’s already been deployed.

If I’m the defender and you give me a particular attack, I can often make changes that stop it. But then if you give the attacker access to that updated defense and let them adapt, they may find another way around it. So you can get apparently contradictory results where the defense succeeds in one experiment and the attack succeeds in another, simply because you changed who got to move last.

For a deployed system, the attacker usually gets to see the system and then choose what to try. That means the relevant test is an adaptive one: after you’ve built your defense, can someone who knows how it works still break it? Stopping a fixed collection of existing attacks is useful, but it’s a much weaker claim than being secure against someone actively trying to get around your particular defense.

r001.rationale: The response says an attacker can adapt to and try to get around the particular deployed defense, rather than needing to defeat every possible defense.

r002.rationale: It explains that an attacker who sees the established system can use that knowledge to adapt and find a way around the defense.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention data poisoning or the defender choosing a defense after poisoned training data is published.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the order matters a lot. If I’m the attacker and I get to see the defense before choosing my attack, I can adapt to whatever you’ve built. You test your defense against some attacks, deploy it, and then I get to spend as long as I want finding something you didn’t anticipate. That’s a pretty substantial advantage.

But you can also reverse that order. If I find an attack and you get to inspect it before deciding how to defend, you can often patch that particular vulnerability. So you can get this back-and-forth where whoever moves last appears to be winning.

The question I care about is whether a defense works against an attacker who knows how it works and is actively trying to break it. Beating the attacks you used to develop the defense is useful, but it’s a much weaker result than surviving that adaptive attacker.

r001.rationale: The response says an attacker who sees the defense can adapt their attack to what was built, identifying the particular defense as the target.

r002.rationale: It explains that after deployment, the attacker can spend time finding an attack the defense designer did not anticipate.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention data poisoning or poisoned training data being published before the defender chooses a defense.
